learn.title: Magic numbers
learn.body: A number like 3.14159 sitting in the middle of code is a magic number. A reader cannot tell what it means, and if you must change it you have to hunt through the program. Giving it a name solves both problems.

learn.title: const and #define
learn.body: `PI` is a macro. `r` is a constant variable.

learn.title: const
learn.body: Putting `const` before a variable makes it read only after its first value is set. If you try to change it later, the compiler reports an error. Use it for values that should never change, such as the number of days in a week.

learn.title: #define
learn.body: `#define PI 3.14159` creates a macro. Before compiling, the preprocessor replaces every `PI` in your code with the text `3.14159`. A macro line has no equals sign and no semicolon. By tradition macro names are in capitals.

learn.title: Which to use
learn.body: Both work for named values. A `const` variable has a type, which helps the compiler catch mistakes, and it follows scope rules. A macro is plain text replacement. In this course use `const` for most things and `#define` for simple named values like a size or a limit.

learn.title: What the program computes
learn.body: The radius is 2 and the area is `PI * r * r`.
steps: `%.2f` rounds to two decimals and prints 12.57

learn.body: Do not end a `#define` with a semicolon. The semicolon becomes part of the replacement text and breaks your code.
